Emberline Spectralis - the manual

Welcome! This is a wavetable synth built for melodic, deep and organic house: warm pads, rolling bass, glassy plucks and the odd stutter-y lead. You don't need to know synth theory to get going. If you can turn a knob, you're sorted.

Start here:

  1. Getting started - install it, make a sound, find your way around
  2. The oscillators - where the sound comes from
  3. Filters, drift and warmth - shaping it and making it less "digital"
  4. Moving things around - LFOs, envelopes, macros and how to hook them up
  5. Effects - distortion, chorus, delay, reverb
  6. Arp and stutter - the arpeggiator and the speed-up/slow-down roll
  7. Presets, saving and sharing - browsing, saving, exporting, crediting
  8. Your own wavetables - drop in WAVs
  9. Recipes - a few classic sounds step by step
  10. Troubleshooting - when something's not right
  11. Knob reference - every control, its range and default

Version: 0.1.0 pre-beta. Things may move around a bit before 1.0.

Getting started

Installing

Windows: unzip the release and copy Emberline Spectralis.vst3 into C:\Program Files\Common Files\VST3. Rescan plugins in your DAW. There's also a Standalone app (Emberline Spectralis.exe) you can just double-click.

Mac: copy Emberline Spectralis.vst3 into /Library/Audio/Plug-Ins/VST3 (or the same folder inside your user Library). The beta builds aren't signed yet, so macOS may grumble the first time. Right-click the file and choose Open, or if it still won't load, run this in Terminal on the plugin: xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine "/Library/Audio/Plug-Ins/VST3/Emberline Spectralis.vst3". On Windows you might see a SmartScreen warning for the same reason: click More info > Run anyway.

It's a VST3 instrument, so load it on a MIDI/instrument track like any other synth.

Your first sound

Load it up and it starts on a preset called Honeyed Keys. Play a few notes. Now:

  1. Click the preset name at the top left and pick something from a category: Pad, Bass, Pluck, Keys... Use the < and > buttons to flick through them one by one.
  2. Turn the CUTOFF knob in the Master panel. That's the filter: left is dark and muffled, right is bright.
  3. Turn M1 to M4 in the Performance Macros box. Most presets wire these up to something fun, so they're the quick way to make a sound your own. The names under the knobs change from preset to preset.

That's honestly most of it. The rest of this manual is about going deeper when you want to.

Finding your way round

The screen has three parts:

  • Top row of chips (LFO 1, ENV 1, M1, CH X...). These are your movers. Drag one onto a knob and the knob starts moving by itself. More on that in Moving things around.
  • The top half: three oscillators (OSC 1-3), the Master panel and the four Macros.
  • The bottom half: six tabs.
  • VISUALIZERS - the LFOs and a live picture of your filter opening and closing.
  • LFOs & CHAOS - draw your own LFO shapes, plus the chaos engine.
  • MOD MATRIX - a list of every connection.
  • FX CHAIN - distortion, chorus, delay, reverb.
  • FILTERS & ENVS - two filters, sub and noise, three envelopes.
  • ARP & STUTTER - the arpeggiator.

Next to the preset bar there's a ? button: click it and choose Open the manual to read this in your web browser (it works offline, the manual lives inside the plugin). The same menu has a link to buy me a coffee if you're enjoying the synth, and so does the little "buy me a coffee" line under the artist credit. Totally optional, always appreciated.

Top right you'll see by and a link: that's who made the preset you're playing. Click it to visit them. Under the preset bar there's the version number.

Handy knob tricks

  • Drag a knob up or down to change it.
  • Double-click a knob to snap it back to its default.
  • Click the little number box under a knob to type a value.
  • Right-click a knob that has movement on it to open its modulation box (see Moving things around).

Using it in your DAW

  • It's a standard VST3 synth, so your DAW's automation, MIDI and presets work as usual. Your DAW remembers the sound in the project, so you can close and reopen without losing anything.
  • The tempo-synced bits (LFOs, delay, arp) follow your DAW's tempo. In the Standalone app, there's a TEMPO knob in the Filters tab instead.
  • Up to 8 notes at once.

The oscillators

An oscillator is the thing that makes the raw sound. Emberline has three, and each one plays a wavetable: a little stack of 16 different waveforms that you can glide through.

The knobs

Each OSC panel has the same set:

Knob What it does
ON Turns the oscillator on or off (OSC 1 is on by default; 2 and 3 you switch on).
Table (the name box) Which wavetable this oscillator uses. Use the arrows, or click it for a list with little pictures of each table.
Warp mode (the box next to it) Bends the wave: Formant, Sync, Bend, Phase Dist, or Off.
FRAME Where you are in the stack. Sweeping this is the classic "wavetable" movement.
WARP How much of the warp mode to apply.
LEVEL How loud this oscillator is.
UNISON How many copies of the sound play at once (1-16). More = thicker, bigger, wider.
DETUNE How far apart those copies are tuned. A little is warm; a lot is supersaw-y.
SPREAD How wide they're spread across the stereo field.
SEMI / FINE Tune the whole oscillator in semitones / in cents.
PAN Pans the oscillator left or right.

The little 3D picture at the top of each panel shows the wavetable, with a bright line for where you are right now. It follows the oscillator it belongs to, so you can see your FRAME movement and the warp as it happens.

Picking a wavetable

There are lots of factory tables. A few ways to think about them:

  • Classic Morph, Saw Sweep, Pulse Width... - the "synthy" ones. Good for basses and leads.
  • Electric Piano, Grand Piano, Clavinet, Tonewheel Organ... - real-instrument-flavoured. Great for keys and organic house.
  • Mallet, Pluck Position, Glass Harmonics, FM Bell... - bells, plucks, glassy things.
  • Cello, Violin, Flute, Human Voice, Vowel Sweep... - organic and vocal.
  • User 1-8 - slots for your own files, see Your own wavetables.

Tip: set FRAME to the middle and give it a slow LFO. Instant movement.

Thickening things up

  • Two oscillators on the same table, one tuned +12 semitones, is a quick way to get a richer sound.
  • UNISON 4-6 with DETUNE around 10-20 gives you a lovely wide pad. Past 40 starts to sound chorusy and out of tune.
  • Want it chunkier at the bottom? Use the Sub in the Filters tab (a clean sine or triangle one or two octaves down). The Noise knob (white, pink or crackle) next to it adds air and grit.

Heads-up on CPU

Lots of unison across all three oscillators with 8 notes held is the heaviest thing the synth can do. It's still well within what a normal computer can cope with, but if your DAW starts crackling, drop the unison first.

Mono, legato and glide (the pitch-slide sound)

By default the synth is polyphonic: play a chord and every note sounds. For basses, leads and those big sliding pitch moves you want one note at a time, and a glide between notes. You'll find these in the VOICE panel on the FILTERS & ENVS tab, and the GLIDE knob is also in the Master panel.

Voice mode

Mode What it does
Poly Normal: play as many notes as you like (up to 8).
Mono One note at a time, and the newest note wins. Every new note retriggers the envelopes, so it sounds like a fresh pluck or stab.
Legato One note at a time, but if you play a note while holding another, the sound just changes pitch without restarting. This is the smooth, singing, slidey one.

In both mono modes, if you let go of the top note while still holding an older one, it drops back to the older note.

Glide (also called portamento) is how long the pitch takes to slide from one note to the next. 0 is off. A few hundredths of a second is a subtle slur; 0.3 s is a lovely slide; 1 s+ is a long dramatic swoop. It always takes the same time whether you jump a tone or two octaves.

Glide mode

  • Always: every note slides from the one before. In Poly mode too, each new note slides from the previous one's pitch.
  • Legato Only: it only slides when you overlap notes (play the next one before letting go of the last). Notes you play separately stay tight. This is great for basslines, because the groove stays punchy and you choose when to slide.

Try this: load Bass - Tidal Slide, play a slow line and hold each note a bit longer than the gap. That's the slide. Then try Bass - Moon Drop for a bigger one, Lead - Sunrise Slide for a singing lead, and Pluck - Unalived Rat for a squelchy mono pluck.

Glide works with the arp too: switch the arp on, set Mono, and the arp line slurs between steps.

Note: the sustain pedal only works in Poly mode.

Filters, drift and warmth

The filters

There are two filters (on the FILTERS & ENVS tab). By default only Filter 1 is on, as a lowpass.

Filter types

Type Sounds like
Lowpass Cuts the top end. The one you'll use most: pads, bass, plucks.
Highpass Cuts the low end. Thins things out, good for risers.
Bandpass Only lets a slice through. Nasal, vocal, "phone" sounds.
Notch Scoops a slice out. Phasey, hollow.
Formant Vowel-like filtering. Talky, vocal.
Ladder A warm, fat, analogue-style 4-pole lowpass. It bites when you push the resonance, then saturates nicely.
Off Bypass.

If your sound feels a bit harsh or metallic, try Ladder. It's the quickest way to get it to sit nicer.

Slope: 12 dB or 24 dB

Next to the type there's a 12 dB / 24 dB switch. It's how steeply the filter cuts. 12 dB is gentle and open; 24 dB is tighter, darker and more obviously "filtery". If you're not sure, try both and trust your ears.

The knobs

  • CUTOFF - where the filter starts to cut (20 Hz to 20 kHz).
  • RESONANCE - a boost right at the cutoff. A little adds character; a lot whistles.
  • DRIVE - pushes more signal into the filter for some grit.

You can also grab CUTOFF and RESONANCE for Filter 1 in the Master panel, so they're always in reach.

Two filters together: Routing

Use the Routing box (in the VOICE / ROUTING panel on the right of the Filters tab):

  • Serial - the sound goes through Filter 1, then Filter 2. Great for a lowpass plus a highpass (a band you can squeeze).
  • Parallel - both filters work on the original sound, then get mixed. Great for two bands, or a notch + something else.

Watching the filter work

The VISUALIZERS tab has a big live picture of the filter curve. You'll see it open and close as the cutoff moves, including anything you've got modulating it, the curve for each filter, and little markers showing the cutoff. It follows the latest note you played, so play a note and watch.

Drift and Warmth (the "analogue" bit)

Digital synths can sound a bit too perfect. Two knobs in the Master panel fix that:

DRIFT - makes the pitch wander very slightly, and makes each note a tiny bit different, like old analogue gear that never quite stays still. At low settings you'll feel it more than hear it: a bit of life and width. At high settings it gets properly wobbly.

WARMTH - gently squashes the loudest peaks (like pushing a tape or a transformer) and rolls off the harsh top end. Turn it up for a softer, darker, fatter sound.

Try this: play a pad, then slowly turn Warmth up. Hear the fizzy top end relax? That's the sweet spot for a deep house chord.

Both are on a little by default (Drift 0.25, Warmth 0.3), so everything sounds a bit warmer out of the box. Too dull? Back off Warmth. Want it totally clean and crisp? Set both to 0.

Presets remember their own Drift and Warmth settings, so you'll notice some sounds are clean and some are dirtier. That's on purpose.

Moving things around (modulation)

"Modulation" just means making a knob move by itself. A filter that slowly opens, a wavetable that drifts, a reverb that swells when you push a wheel. This is what makes a patch feel alive, and it's a big part of the deep house sound.

The movers

They're the coloured chips along the top of the screen:

Chip What it is
LFO 1-3 (purple) Slow repeating waves. Wobble, sweep, pulse. You can draw your own shapes.
ENV 1-3 (red/orange) Envelopes: shapes that play out each time you hit a note. ENV 1 is also your volume envelope.
M1-M4 (cyan) The four Macro knobs. You control these by hand (or with your DAW's automation).
CH X / Y / Z (gold) The chaos engine: smooth, never-repeating wandering.
PERLIN (gold) Smooth, organic random drift.
S&H (gold) Sample-and-hold: random steps.
VEL (green) How hard you hit the key.
KEY (green) Which key you played (low to high).
WHEEL (green) Your mod wheel.
AFTER (green) Aftertouch (pressing into the key).
RAND (green) A new random number for each note.

Hooking one up: drag and drop

  1. Drag a chip from the top row.
  2. Drop it on a knob (any knob with a little ring around it).
  3. A small box pops up right there. Set DEPTH to how much you want it to move that knob.

That's it. You never need to leave the screen you're on.

In the box you can also:

  • CURVE - bend how the movement feels (more at the start or more at the end).
  • BIPOLAR - lets the mover push the knob both up and down from where it sits, instead of only one way.
  • X (remove) - take the connection away.

To open that box again later, right-click the knob. If the knob has several movers on it, you'll get one row for each.

Round the knob, you'll see a coloured ring showing how far the movement reaches, and it animates live as the sound plays.

The three LFOs

On the LFOs & CHAOS tab you'll find LFO 1, 2 and 3, each with a shape you can draw:

  • Drag the dots to move points. Drag the little diamond between two points to bend that stretch of the line.
  • Double-click the line to add a point, or double-click a point to remove it.
  • Right-click for a menu of ready-made shapes to start from.
  • RATE sets how fast it goes. The little box next to it ("Off" by default) lets you sync to tempo instead: pick a note length (1/4, 1/8., 1 bar, 4 bars...) and it stays locked to your DAW.
  • Retrig / Free - Retrig restarts the shape on every note; Free just keeps running.

The chaos engine

The Lorenz chaos engine draws a looping, never-quite-repeating path. It gives you three outputs (CH X, Y, Z). Use it for subtle, organic movement that doesn't sound like an LFO going round and round. LORENZ RATE sets its speed. FRACTAL RATE (right next to it) sets how fast the Perlin and S&H movers run.

Envelopes

On the FILTERS & ENVS tab, three envelopes with the usual ATK (attack), DEC (decay), SUS (sustain), REL (release), plus A CRV and D CRV to bend the attack and decay curves.

ENV 1 controls the overall volume of each note. ENV 2 and 3 are free for you to use on anything. The classic trick: hook ENV 2 up to the filter cutoff for a pluck.

The macros

M1-M4 are your four performance knobs. Presets name them (Brightness, Morph, Space, Width...) and wire them up to useful things. You can rewire them yourself by dragging the macro chips onto any knob.

The Mod Matrix

The MOD MATRIX tab is a list of every connection in the preset (16 at most). Each row is Source -> Destination, with depth, curve and bipolar controls. It's the same thing as dropping chips on knobs, just in a list. It's handy for checking what's going on and for tidying things up.

Some ideas to try

  • Slow filter breathing: LFO 1 at about 0.2 Hz (or synced to 1 bar) -> Filter 1 Cutoff, small depth.
  • Movement in the wavetable: LFO 2 -> OSC 1 Frame, tiny depth.
  • Pluck: ENV 2 -> Filter 1 Cutoff, decent depth, short decay and no sustain.
  • Played harder = brighter: Velocity -> Filter 1 Cutoff.
  • Organic wobble: Perlin -> OSC 1 Fine or OSC 1 Pan, tiny depth.
  • One-knob drops: Macro 1 -> Filter Cutoff, Reverb Mix and Delay Mix all at once, then automate Macro 1 in your DAW.

Effects

Four effects, on the FX CHAIN tab: Distortion, Chorus/Flanger, Delay and Reverb. Each one has its own ON tick box, so only the ones you use cost you any CPU.

Changing the order

The numbers 1-4 on the panels are the running order. Drag a panel's header left or right to reorder them. For example: reverb before delay gives you a washy echo; delay before reverb gives you clean echoes that sit in a room.

Distortion

Knob What it does
Type Soft (gentle), Hard (aggressive), Fold (wavefolding, metallic), Tube (warm).
DRIVE How hard it's pushed.
TONE Dark to bright.
MIX Blend of dry and distorted.

Tip: Tube at a low drive is a nice cheap way to warm a pad.

Chorus / Flanger

Knob What it does
Mode Chorus (wide and shimmery) or Flanger (jet-plane swoosh).
RATE How fast it wobbles.
DEPTH How much it wobbles.
FEEDBACK Mostly for the flanger: more feedback = more metallic ring.
MIX Blend.

Delay

Knob What it does
Sync box Off uses the TIME knob in milliseconds. Pick a note length (1/8., 1/4, ...) and it locks to your DAW's tempo.
TIME Delay time in ms when sync is Off.
FEEDBACK How many repeats. High values go on for ages.
TONE Darkens each repeat. Lower = more tape-like.
MIX Blend.

For melodic house, a dotted-eighth (1/8.) delay is the classic.

Reverb

Knob What it does
SIZE Room size.
DECAY How long the tail lasts (up to 20 seconds).
DAMPING How quickly the high end dies away in the tail. Higher = darker and smoother.
MIX Blend.

Tip: for pads, a big DECAY (4-8 s) with some DAMPING gives that lush, wide wash. For plucks, keep the decay short.

Arp and stutter

The ARP & STUTTER tab has a built-in arpeggiator, with a roll-style stutter that speeds up and slows down. It's off until you tick ON, so nothing changes in your old patches.

The arpeggiator

Switch it on, hold a chord, and instead of playing together, the notes play one at a time. It's locked to your DAW's tempo and transport, so it stays in time with everything else.

Control What it does
ON Arp on/off.
Mode The order the notes play in: Up, Down, Up/Down, Down/Up, Up/Down Repeat, Converge, Diverge, Random, As Played, or Chord (everything at once, rhythmically).
Rate How fast: 1/32, 1/16 (default), triplets (T), dotted (.), up to 1/4.
Pattern A rhythm over 16 steps: All Steps, Rolling, Offbeat, Syncopated, Gallop, Skip, Push, Half Time, Dotted. The bars above show which steps play, and tall bars are accents.
LATCH Keeps playing after you let go. Play a new chord and it swaps over. Great for hands-free grooves.
OCTAVES Stretches the pattern up 1-4 octaves.
GATE How long each note rings: short and staccato to long and legato.
SWING Pushes every other step late for a shuffle.
ACCENT How much louder the accent steps are.
HUMANISE Random little differences in velocity so it feels played, not programmed.

Start with Up, 1/16, All Steps, then try the patterns. Rolling and Offbeat are lovely for deep house.

Stutter (the speed-up / slow-down roll)

Stutter changes the arp's speed over time, which is the classic build-up and "ball drop" trick. The panel on the right draws what's happening.

Control What it does
Mode Off, Speed Up (starts slow and builds into a roll, like 1/8 > 1/16 > 1/32), Slow Down (starts fast and falls away, like a bouncing ball), or Up & Down (speeds up then slows back).
Length How long one speed-up/slow-down takes: 1/2 bar, 1 bar, 2 bars or 4 bars. It repeats.
Curve Smooth glides the speed. Stepped snaps to neat musical speeds (doubling each time) so it stays on the grid.
DEPTH How extreme it gets. A little is a subtle push; a lot gets right up to a machine-gun roll.

While it's rolling quickly, the notes also get louder as they speed up, so it swells into the drop. And when it's going fast, the pattern and swing are ignored so the roll stays clean.

Try this: - Speed Up, 2 bars, Stepped, depth about 0.5, on a held chord at the end of a 4-bar phrase. Instant build. - Slow Down, 1 bar, Smooth, on a single bass note for a bouncing-ball drop. - Automate the Mode or DEPTH in your DAW to do fills only when you want them.

Presets that use it

Try these: Rolling Gold, Offbeat Orchard, Stutter Rise, Ball Drop, Heartbeat Sway, Pulse Garden Stutter, Moonlit Cascade (that one's latched, so just play a chord and walk away).

Good to know

  • When the DAW transport is playing, the arp locks to the beat. When it's stopped, it free-runs at the tempo.
  • Turning the arp off while notes are playing won't leave stuck notes.

Presets, saving and sharing

Browsing

The preset bar is at the top left: [ < ] [ name ] [ > ] [ SAVE ].

  • < and > step through every preset one by one.
  • Click the name to open a menu with all the presets sorted by type: Bass, Pluck, Lead, Pad, Keys, Chord, Arp, Organic, Texture, FX and your own (USER).

Every preset starts from a clean slate, so a preset never picks up leftovers from the sound before it.

Who made it

Presets can carry a name and a link, shown top right as by with the link underneath. Click it to open it in your browser. For more detail, open the preset menu and choose Preset info... to see the author, link, description and tags. The link only ever opens normal web addresses.

Saving your own

  1. Make a sound you like.
  2. Click SAVE.
  3. Fill in the box:
  4. Name - what you'll call it.
  5. Category - where it lives in the menu (USER by default).
  6. Description - a line or two on what it sounds like or when to use it.
  7. Tags - a few words, separated by commas (e.g. warm, pad, melodic).
  8. Author / artist name and Link - your name and your Instagram, website or anywhere you want people to find you. The synth remembers these for next time, so you only type them once.
  9. Click Save.

Your preset is saved as a plain text file in your user folder, and shows up in the menu straight away:

  • Windows: %APPDATA%\Emberline\Spectralis\Presets\
  • Mac: ~/Library/Application Support/Emberline/Spectralis/Presets/
  • Linux: ~/.config/Emberline/Spectralis/Presets/

The menu has Show user preset folder to jump straight there, and Rescan user presets if you've been adding files by hand.

Sharing a preset

Open the preset menu:

  • Export current sound as .json... - saves the sound you're hearing to a file wherever you like, ready to send to a mate. It keeps the author, link and description of the preset you started from (or yours, if you've saved it). If your sound uses one of your own wavetables, you'll get a reminder: send that file as well, because it isn't stored inside the preset.
  • Import preset file(s)... - pick one or more .json files someone sent you. They land in your user folder and appear in the menu. Nothing gets overwritten, so if the name already exists it just gets a number added.

You can also drop a .json file straight into the presets folder and hit Rescan user presets.

Making presets for the library

Want to make presets for the factory library? Brilliant. See CONTRIBUTING. In short: make it, credit yourself in the save box, export it and send it over.

Editing the files by hand

Presets are readable text (JSON), so you can open one in any text editor and change a number if you fancy. The format is explained in docs/PRESETS.md. If you break a file, it just gets ignored. It won't crash anything.

Your own wavetables

You can feed the synth your own sounds. Anything you load turns up in the table list of every oscillator as User 1 to User 8.

The easy way: import from the table list

  1. Click the table name on any oscillator to open the list.
  2. At the bottom choose Import wavetable (.wav / .json)... and pick your file(s). They're copied into your user folder for you, and the new table gets selected straight away.
  3. The list also has Rescan wavetable folder and Show wavetable folder.

Your files fill the User 1-8 slots in alphabetical order.

Or drop the files in yourself

  1. Put a .wav file in your user wavetable folder:
  2. Windows: %APPDATA%\Emberline\Spectralis\Wavetables\
  3. Mac: ~/Library/Application Support/Emberline/Spectralis/Wavetables/
  4. Linux: ~/.config/Emberline/Spectralis/Wavetables/
  5. In any oscillator's table list, choose Rescan wavetable folder (or just restart).
  6. Pick User 1 or whichever slot your file landed in.

What kind of WAV works?

  • A "wavetable" WAV (the kind Serum and Vital use): a file made of several frames of 2048 samples each. It gets squeezed into 16 frames and you sweep through them with FRAME.
  • A single cycle of any length (for example from AKWF packs): used as one waveform.
  • Stereo files are mixed to mono.

The first 8 files (alphabetical) get the slots. Rename them with numbers if you want to control the order.

Wavetables as text

Wavetables can also be written as text (.json): you describe harmonics or shapes and the synth builds the table. That's more of a nerd thing, and it's explained in docs/WAVETABLES.md. You can also paste that guide into an AI chat to get it to write wavetables for you.

Sharing

A preset that uses your own wavetable only works for someone else if they've got the same file. Send both! Make sure you've got the rights to share any samples you didn't make yourself.

Recipes

Starting points to bend into your own thing. Numbers are a guide: trust your ears, not the numbers.

All of these start from the default sound; use Init - Basic Saw (in the Init category) if you'd like a blank page.

Warm deep-house chord pad

  1. OSC 1: pick Saw Sweep or Blended Waves. UNISON 4, DETUNE around 12, SPREAD 0.6.
  2. Switch OSC 2 on, same table, SEMI 0, DETUNE a touch different.
  3. Filter 1: Ladder, 24 dB, CUTOFF about 2.5 kHz, RESONANCE low.
  4. ENV 1: slow ATK (0.3 s), long REL (1.2 s).
  5. Drag LFO 1 onto Filter 1 CUTOFF, small DEPTH, RATE synced to 1 bar for a slow breathe.
  6. FX: a touch of Chorus, then Reverb with DECAY about 5 s. Turn WARMTH to about 0.4.

Rolling sub bass

  1. OSC 1: Digital Bass or Bass Weight, UNISON 1.
  2. Sub at about 0.5 (sine, -1 Oct).
  3. Filter 1: Lowpass, 24 dB, CUTOFF low (about 400 Hz).
  4. ENV 2 onto CUTOFF for a short pluck on each note (short DEC, SUS 0).
  5. Short REL on ENV 1 for a tight bass.
  6. Add a touch of Distortion (Tube) for presence.

The pitch-slide bassline

  1. Voice panel: Legato, glide mode Legato Only, GLIDE about 0.3 s.
  2. OSC 1: Bass Weight; Sub about 0.4; Filter 1 Ladder, 24 dB, CUTOFF around 400 Hz.
  3. Play a long, slow line and overlap each note into the next. Short, separate notes stay punchy; overlapped ones slide.
  4. For a bigger swoop use Mono with GLIDE at 0.5 s or more and glide mode Always.
  5. Try it with the arp: set Mono and a slow rate, and the line glides between steps.

Glassy pluck

  1. OSC 1: Mallet or Glass Harmonics.
  2. ENV 1: short DEC (0.3 s), SUS 0.
  3. Filter 1: Lowpass, CUTOFF about 5 kHz, ENV 2 onto cutoff, small depth.
  4. Delay: sync 1/8., FEEDBACK about 0.4, MIX about 0.25. Reverb on the side.

Evolving organic lead

  1. OSC 1: Flute, Cello or Human Voice.
  2. Drag Perlin onto OSC 1 FRAME and onto FINE with a tiny depth.
  3. Velocity onto Filter 1 CUTOFF, so harder notes are brighter.
  4. Mod Wheel onto Reverb Mix for a swell.

Rolling arp with a stutter build

  1. Load any pluck or keys sound. Go to ARP & STUTTER, tick ON.
  2. Mode Up, 1/16, Pattern Rolling, OCTAVES 2.
  3. Stutter mode Speed Up, Length 2 bars, Curve Stepped, DEPTH 0.5.
  4. Hold a chord for 8 bars and automate stutter Mode to Off for the drop.

One-knob build-up

  1. Pick M1, and drag its chip onto Filter 1 CUTOFF, Reverb Mix and Delay Mix (right-click each knob to set depths).
  2. Automate M1 in your DAW from 0 to 1 over 8 bars.

Troubleshooting

My DAW doesn't see the plugin. Check that Emberline Spectralis.vst3 is in your VST3 folder (Windows: C:\Program Files\Common Files\VST3) and rescan plugins. Some DAWs only rescan if you tell them to.

Mac says it can't be opened / is from an unidentified developer. The beta isn't signed yet. Right-click the plugin, choose Open, or in Terminal: xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine "/Library/Audio/Plug-Ins/VST3/Emberline Spectralis.vst3" (change the path if you put it elsewhere).

Windows shows a SmartScreen warning. Same reason. Click More info, then Run anyway.

No sound. Make sure the track is getting MIDI and is armed. Check that OSC 1 is switched on and its LEVEL is up, and that the VOLUME knob in the Master panel isn't right down. If you've got the arp on, you need to hold a chord (or turn on LATCH).

Crackling or dropouts. Raise your DAW's audio buffer size (256 or 512 is fine for jamming). Lower the UNISON on the oscillators and switch off any effects you're not using. Lots of unison on all three oscillators is the heaviest thing it does.

I only hear one note when I play a chord. The Voice mode is on Mono or Legato (Filters & Envs tab, VOICE panel). Set it back to Poly for chords.

Notes slide into each other and I don't want that. Turn GLIDE down to 0, or set glide mode to Legato Only so it only slides when notes overlap.

It sounds too dull / too clean / too harsh. That's the WARMTH and DRIFT knobs in the Master panel (more warmth = softer and darker, 0 = clean). If it's still harsh, try the Ladder filter, or pull down the filter CUTOFF.

The arp isn't in time with my song. It follows your DAW's tempo and transport when it's playing. If you jump around the timeline it re-locks to the beat. In the Standalone app there's no DAW, so it uses the TEMPO knob in the Filters tab.

The arp keeps playing after I let go. LATCH is on. Turn it off (or play new notes to replace the held chord).

A preset I downloaded loads but sounds different. It may use one of the author's own wavetables. Ask them to send the wavetable file as well, and see Your own wavetables.

My saved preset isn't in the menu. Open the preset menu and choose Rescan user presets. (For wavetables it's Rescan wavetable folder in the oscillator's table list.) If you saved it by hand, check that the file ends in .json and is valid JSON. (A broken file is skipped quietly.)

Where are my files? - Windows: %APPDATA%\Emberline\Spectralis\ (Presets and Wavetables folders) - Mac: ~/Library/Application Support/Emberline/Spectralis/ - Linux: ~/.config/Emberline/Spectralis/

Something's properly broken. Tell us! Open an issue on the project page with your DAW, operating system, the plugin version (under the preset bar) and what you did.

Knob reference

Every control in the synth, with its range and where it starts. Generated by tools/manual_reference.py, so don't edit by hand.

Controls on the three oscillators, filters, LFOs and envelopes repeat for each number, so only the first is listed in full.

The modulation matrix has 16 rows (source, destination, depth, curve, bipolar); those are covered in Moving things around.
